categories.label: Research & thinking
categories.title: Think it through. Check the claim.
categories.intro: These tools help you explore ideas, understand information, and draft work. Their features overlap; choose around the task and the evidence you need.
categories.decision: For factual decisions, open the original sources. Fluent writing and visible citations are not proof.

tools.name: ChatGPT
tools.summary: A conversational workspace for drafting, analysis, and research.
tools.bestFit: You want to develop an idea, work through files, or investigate a question.
pros: Several kinds of thinking in one workspace.
Follow-up questions let you refine the task.
cons: Capabilities and allowances depend on the account.
Verify factual claims and review generated output.
tools.firstTask: Try one small task with test data before connecting your live workflow.
tools.costNote: Check current plans, included allowances, and usage charges.

tools.name: Claude
tools.summary: A conversational AI workspace, distinct from Claude Code.
tools.bestFit: You want to work through writing, documents, or an idea.
pros: Useful for working through a draft in stages.
Documents and conversation can share context.
cons: Claude chat and Claude Code have different working environments.
Generated content still needs your review.
tools.firstTask: Try one small task with test data before connecting your live workflow.
tools.costNote: Check current plans, included allowances, and usage charges.

tools.name: Perplexity
tools.summary: An AI search and research tool that links to sources.
tools.bestFit: You want a sourced starting point for an unfamiliar subject.
pros: Sources are visible for further inspection.
Research can be refined through conversation.
cons: A linked source may not support the exact claim.
Advanced research allowances vary by plan.
tools.firstTask: Try one small task with test data before connecting your live workflow.
tools.costNote: Check current plans, included allowances, and usage charges.

tools.name: Gemini
tools.summary: Google’s conversational AI assistant.
tools.bestFit: You want a general AI assistant and supported Google connections.
pros: Another approach to the same writing and thinking tasks.
Google connections may fit an existing workflow.
cons: Connections and features depend on account and region.
Gemini the assistant is different from AI Studio Build mode.
tools.firstTask: Try one small task with test data before connecting your live workflow.
tools.costNote: Check current plans, included allowances, and usage charges.

categories.label: Guided app builders
categories.title: Build from a prompt
categories.intro: Guided builders bring code generation, preview, and supporting services into one environment. They overlap with AI editors: both can help create complete apps.
categories.decision: Compare the workflow, supported stack, code access, publishing, and cost—not just whether the tool can build an app.
categories.note: A guided builder is not limited to prototypes. A code editor is not limited to editing. Neither guarantees a finished, tested product.

tools.name: Lovable
tools.summary: A natural-language platform for building and publishing web applications.
tools.bestFit: You want a guided web-app workflow with code access and publishing options.
features: Editable application code and Git sync
pros: Useful for turning a concept into something you can inspect.
Git sync provides a route into an external development workflow.
cons: Generated apps still need real behavior and access checks.
Build credits and operating services can have separate costs.
tools.firstTask: Prototype one screen without login, payment, or sensitive data.
tools.costNote: Credit-based plans; check hosting and backend usage separately.

tools.name: Replit Agent
tools.summary: An app-building Agent in an integrated development platform.
tools.bestFit: You want a managed workspace rather than setting up everything locally.
pros: Planning and implementation can happen in one environment.
Checkpoints provide a way to revisit earlier project states.
cons: Agent work and running the published app are separate cost considerations.
Moving an app elsewhere requires reviewing its service dependencies.
tools.firstTask: Plan one small app, approve a narrow task, then test the output yourself.
tools.costNote: Plan allowances and paid Agent modes vary; review publishing costs separately.

tools.name: Bolt
tools.summary: A prompt-driven builder focused on JavaScript-based applications.
tools.bestFit: You want to prototype a JavaScript web app in the browser.
features: Bolt Cloud database or Supabase connection
pros: A browser-based workflow reduces local setup for a prototype.
A supported database path is available alongside app building.
cons: It is not a general-purpose Python or PHP backend environment.
Backend choice, plan limits, and publication still need review.
tools.firstTask: Build one simple screen, then check the supported stack before expanding it.
tools.costNote: Review current build limits and cloud-service costs before subscribing.

tools.name: Google AI Studio
tools.summary: An AI development workspace with a prompt-driven Build mode.
tools.bestFit: You want to build and test an app, particularly one using Gemini.
pros: Build and inspect generated code in one environment.
Export provides a path to local development.
cons: Model usage and deployment may have separate costs.
Review secrets, access rules, and generated behavior.
tools.firstTask: Try one small task with test data before connecting your live workflow.
tools.costNote: Check current plans, included allowances, and usage charges.

tools.name: FlutterFlow
tools.summary: A visual development platform for Flutter-based apps.
tools.bestFit: You want visual screen design for a Flutter app.
pros: Visual controls provide another way to construct screens.
Flutter provides a path toward multi-platform apps.
cons: Code export and advanced features depend on the plan.
Custom behavior and platform testing still require work.
tools.firstTask: Try one small task with test data before connecting your live workflow.
tools.costNote: Check current plans, included allowances, and usage charges.

categories.label: Editors & coding Agents
categories.title: Build with the project in your hands
categories.intro: An AI editor can help create an app from scratch as well as inspect an existing one. Coding Agents can work inside an editor or through other environments.
categories.decision: Start with one main working environment. Compare how you inspect changes, run checks, connect services, and publish.
categories.note: Cursor is the editor and includes an Agent. Claude Code is a coding Agent. They can be used together; switching requires a clear handoff and coordinated edits.

tools.name: Cursor
tools.summary: An editor with an integrated coding Agent.
tools.bestFit: You want to build or change an app while working directly with its project files.
pros: AI work and code review share one workspace.
Project instructions help keep recurring tasks consistent.
cons: Agent usage and model access depend on the plan.
Checkpoints undo Agent edits; they do not replace permanent Git history.
Review the diff and test the actual behavior before accepting done.
tools.firstTask: Ask it to explain one component without editing any files.
tools.costNote: Free entry plan with limits; paid plans and additional usage.

tools.name: VS Code + GitHub Copilot
tools.summary: A general code editor with Copilot-powered AI features.
tools.bestFit: You want a familiar editor and a choice of extensions.
pros: You can keep editing without relying on one AI feature.
A broad extension system lets you tailor the workspace.
cons: Editor setup and Copilot account setup are separate choices.
AI allowances and capabilities vary by plan and organization settings.
tools.firstTask: Open a small project and ask Copilot to explain its structure.
tools.costNote: The editor is free; Copilot has separate plans and usage limits.

tools.name: Devin Desktop (Windsurf successor)
tools.summary: An editor and command center for local and cloud coding agents.
tools.bestFit: You want agent session management alongside a full editor.
features: Integrated editor and agent command center
pros: Agent sessions and code inspection stay together.
Cascade offers a path for both questions and implementation.
cons: More agent-management controls can add complexity for a first project.
Check the current plan and account requirements before switching.
tools.firstTask: Use Cascade to explain a component; inspect its answer before requesting an edit.
tools.costNote: Check the current product plans; legacy Windsurf terms may differ.

tools.name: Claude Code
tools.summary: A coding Agent that works across project files and development tools.
tools.bestFit: You want task-focused work in your terminal, editor, app, or browser.
pros: Several working environments let you keep your existing setup.
Project instructions provide a place for recurring guidance.
cons: Permissions and instructions need review before implementation.
A separate tool can mean separate usage and handoff requirements.
tools.firstTask: Ask it to read project instructions and propose a plan before editing.
tools.costNote: Account, subscription, or provider usage requirements vary by environment.

tools.name: OpenAI Codex
tools.summary: An Agent for writing, reviewing, and working with code.
tools.bestFit: You want an OpenAI coding workflow in an editor, terminal, or supported app.
features: Permission controls and cloud tasks where eligible
pros: Several clients provide different ways into the same family of tools.
You can review task output and code changes in your workflow.
cons: Local and cloud access are not identical across accounts.
Usage limits, permissions, and available clients depend on your setup.
tools.firstTask: Ask for a read-only explanation of a small bug and a proposed fix.
tools.costNote: Plan-based usage varies; API-key use has separate billing.

categories.label: App frameworks
categories.title: Choose what the app is built with
categories.intro: A framework provides the structure used to make an app. It is a different layer from an editor or a prompt-driven builder.
categories.decision: For this text-rich personal-brand website, keep the existing web approach. Compare mobile frameworks when you have a mobile-app requirement.
categories.note: Flutter is the framework; FlutterFlow is a visual builder that works with Flutter. React Native and React for the web are also different choices.

tools.name: Flutter
tools.summary: A Dart-based framework for multi-platform applications.
tools.bestFit: You want a shared codebase with mobile apps central to the project.
features: Android, iOS, web, and desktop targets
pros: Much application code can be shared.
Flexible control over the interface.
cons: Dart and Flutter have their own learning curve.
Each platform needs testing; text-heavy marketing sites are a poor fit.
tools.firstTask: Run one screen on the intended device before expanding the project.
tools.costNote: Free and open source; hosting, stores, services, and development still have costs.

tools.name: React Native + Expo
tools.summary: A mobile-app framework with Expo’s development and deployment tooling.
tools.bestFit: You want a React and JavaScript/TypeScript route to mobile apps.
pros: A useful route for a team already working with React.
Expo bundles common mobile development tools.
cons: Web React code is not automatically a complete native app.
Native requirements and cloud services can add complexity and cost.
tools.firstTask: Try one small task with test data before connecting your live workflow.
tools.costNote: Check current plans, included allowances, and usage charges.

categories.label: Backends
categories.title: Save data and manage access
categories.intro: A backend stores information and controls who can use it. Choose it around your data, permissions, and operating needs.
categories.decision: Compare the data model first. Changing backend providers later usually means changing application code, permissions, and migration plans.
categories.note: Signing in proves identity. Access rules determine which records a signed-in person can read or change.

tools.name: Supabase
tools.summary: A Postgres-based backend with authentication and file storage.
tools.bestFit: Your data has relationships, and you want a SQL database.
pros: SQL gives you a clear way to query related data.
Database, sign-in, and storage are available in one platform.
cons: Row Level Security must be designed and tested.
Cloud quotas, project costs, and backup coverage need review.
Keep privileged server-side keys out of browser code.
tools.firstTask: Map who can read and change each record, then test two different users.
tools.costNote: Free and paid cloud plans; compute, storage, and other usage affect cost.

tools.name: Firebase
tools.summary: Google’s app platform with database, sign-in, storage, and hosting services.
tools.bestFit: You want managed app services, particularly realtime or mobile workflows.
features: Firestore document database and offline support
SQL Connect for a managed PostgreSQL route
pros: Firestore supports realtime sync and offline app behavior.
The platform brings several app services together.
cons: Firestore models data differently from a relational SQL database.
Service-specific rules, usage charges, and Google Cloud configuration need attention.
tools.firstTask: Choose Firestore or SQL Connect deliberately; test user access before importing real data.
tools.costNote: Free allowances and usage-based services; check each service’s billing requirements.

tools.name: Appwrite
tools.summary: A backend platform with managed cloud and self-hosting options.
tools.bestFit: You want a bundled backend and the option to operate it yourself.
pros: Several backend jobs share one API-oriented platform.
Self-hosting gives you an infrastructure choice.
cons: Self-hosting adds updates, scaling, security, and backup work.
Its APIs and permission model are not a drop-in Supabase replacement.
tools.firstTask: Start with a test project and verify which user can read one private record.
tools.costNote: Cloud plans have limits; self-hosting still has infrastructure and operating costs.

categories.label: Git & history
categories.title: Record and inspect changes
categories.intro: Git keeps recorded versions of project files. A visual Git client helps you use that history. These are different layers of the same workflow.
categories.decision: Learn what status, diff, commit, and push mean. Then choose the interface that makes those actions easiest to understand.
categories.note: Git is the version-control engine. GitHub Desktop, Sourcetree, and GitKraken are clients for using it. GitHub and GitLab host repositories; they are not replacements for Git.

tools.name: Git
tools.summary: The underlying version-control system for project files.
tools.bestFit: You need recorded changes and separate branches of work.
pros: Local history does not require a hosting subscription.
Many editors and visual clients work with the same repository.
cons: Uncommitted edits are not a saved version.
Git history does not automatically back up a hosted database or untracked media.
tools.firstTask: Inspect status and diff; make an intentional commit after reviewing what it includes.
tools.costNote: Free, open-source software; repository hosting is a separate decision.

tools.name: GitHub Desktop
tools.summary: A visual Git client with a straightforward commit-and-sync workflow.
tools.bestFit: You want fewer terminal commands for everyday Git work.
pros: The visual workflow can make changes easier to inspect.
It works alongside your existing code editor.
cons: Official releases are for Windows and macOS.
Advanced Git tasks may still call for another interface or the terminal.
tools.firstTask: Open a test repository and review the diff before committing a small change.
tools.costNote: Free, open-source client; hosting limits are separate.

categories.label: Application email
categories.title: Send the emails your app owes people
categories.intro: Password resets, confirmations, and download messages need a delivery service connected to your application.
categories.decision: Test a real message and the failure path. A successful API response does not guarantee inbox placement.
categories.note: Email delivery, newsletter management, and an email inbox are different jobs. SMTP is a sending protocol; it is not a competing product. Mailbox provider: VJ to confirm before publication.

tools.name: Resend
tools.summary: An email delivery platform with API, SMTP, and marketing capabilities.
tools.bestFit: You are connecting email delivery to a custom website or app.
pros: Fits a custom application workflow.
Supports sending through API or SMTP.
cons: Verify the sending domain and handle failures and bounces.
A delivery service does not by itself build your entire custom CRM or preference system.
tools.firstTask: Send a test download email; verify the link and delivery event.
tools.costNote: Check current plans, included allowances, and usage charges.

tools.name: Postmark
tools.summary: An application email service with transactional and broadcast streams.
tools.bestFit: You want delivery and tracking for messages triggered by your app.
pros: Message streams distinguish operational and bulk sending.
Templates can be maintained separately from application code.
cons: Sender verification and stream selection require setup.
Your application must still process errors and delivery events.
tools.firstTask: Try one small task with test data before connecting your live workflow.
tools.costNote: Check current plans, included allowances, and usage charges.

tools.name: Twilio SendGrid
tools.summary: An email platform with developer sending and marketing products.
tools.bestFit: You want API-driven delivery and optional campaign tooling.
pros: Can support both developer and marketing workflows.
Integration documentation covers sending and tracking.
cons: Products and plans need separate review.
Authentication, list quality, and delivery monitoring remain your responsibility.
tools.firstTask: Try one small task with test data before connecting your live workflow.
tools.costNote: Check current plans, included allowances, and usage charges.

categories.label: Newsletters
categories.title: Manage the audience and the message
categories.intro: A newsletter platform manages subscribers, campaigns, and follow-up sequences. Your custom interface can use a delivery provider underneath.
categories.decision: Compare topic preferences, unsubscribe handling, segmentation, editor controls, and ongoing maintenance.
categories.note: VJ is building a custom newsletter system with Resend. Describe it as in development until its signup, preference, sending, and unsubscribe paths are verified. Do not imply it is available as a product.

tools.name: Mailchimp
tools.summary: A hosted marketing platform with campaign and audience tools.
tools.bestFit: You want a managed campaign workspace rather than building your own.
pros: Campaign and audience tools are bundled.
Managed features reduce the amount of custom software to maintain.
cons: Plan limits and contact-based costs need review.
Existing preferences and consent need deliberate migration.
tools.firstTask: Try one small task with test data before connecting your live workflow.
tools.costNote: Check current plans, included allowances, and usage charges.

tools.name: Kit
tools.summary: A creator-focused email marketing platform.
tools.bestFit: You publish regularly and want subscriber tools and sequences.
pros: Creator-oriented tools support publishing workflows.
Tags and sequences can organize follow-up.
cons: Advanced capabilities vary by plan.
Contact growth affects the plan decision.
tools.firstTask: Try one small task with test data before connecting your live workflow.
tools.costNote: Check current plans, included allowances, and usage charges.

tools.name: Brevo
tools.summary: A marketing platform with email and automation capabilities.
tools.bestFit: You want email campaigns with broader messaging options.
pros: Several marketing functions share a platform.
Supports workflows beyond a single newsletter.
cons: Breadth adds setup decisions.
Channel availability and allowances depend on the plan.
tools.firstTask: Try one small task with test data before connecting your live workflow.
tools.costNote: Check current plans, included allowances, and usage charges.

categories.label: Automation
categories.title: Connect the work. Cut the repetition.
categories.intro: Automation connects an event in one tool to actions in others. It can move approved content into a publishing workflow.
categories.decision: Start with one trigger and one destination. Check permissions, duplicates, failures, and how you stop the workflow.
categories.note: VJ uses Make to automate posts. The exact source, publishing destination, and approval step have not been specified; do not invent that workflow.

tools.name: Make
tools.summary: A visual automation platform that connects services through scenarios.
tools.bestFit: You want to automate a posting workflow or move information between tools.
pros: Connections and data movement are visible.
Can coordinate several tools in a publishing process.
cons: Platform permissions and connector limits still apply.
Unexpected repeats or bad mappings can publish the wrong content.
tools.firstTask: Use a test post and confirm the destination and approval step before enabling a schedule.
tools.costNote: Check current plans, included allowances, and usage charges.

tools.name: Zapier
tools.summary: A managed automation platform using triggers and actions.
tools.bestFit: You want to connect commonly used services with a hosted workflow.
pros: Managed operation avoids running your own server.
Integration choices can suit straightforward workflows.
cons: Premium features and task allowances depend on the plan.
Multi-step volume changes the cost calculation.
tools.firstTask: Try one small task with test data before connecting your live workflow.
tools.costNote: Check current plans, included allowances, and usage charges.

tools.name: n8n
tools.summary: A workflow automation platform with cloud and self-hosting options.
tools.bestFit: You want flexible workflows and a choice about where they run.
pros: Custom logic can extend a workflow.
Self-hosting is an operating option.
cons: Self-hosting adds maintenance, security, and backup work.
Review its license and service costs; it is not unrestricted open-source software.
tools.firstTask: Try one small task with test data before connecting your live workflow.
tools.costNote: Cloud plans or self-hosting costs; paid capabilities and license conditions vary.

updates.title: The full workflow is now on the shelf
updates.body: Added research, frameworks, email, newsletters, and automation. Make and Resend are confirmed tools in VJ’s stack.

updates.title: Windsurf naming updated
updates.body: Listed Devin Desktop as the successor to Windsurf, with current Cascade documentation.

updates.title: Firebase comparison clarified
updates.body: Separated Firestore’s document model from the PostgreSQL option now documented as SQL Connect.
